doc_summary: Buck and Ryan propose meta-level adversarial evaluation: training red-team policies that fool an oversight process on analogous, checkable proxy failures, to measure whether oversight is locally adequate. They stress constructing proxy settings with the same core difficulty as the real failure, and explicitly do not require hiding the eval from the model.

items.claim: Prefers testing proxy failures that retain the core difficulty of the real bad action (with an observable endpoint) over arbitrary or easier proxies, because the proxy is only valid if the model can do it iff it could do the real failure.
items.quote: This is an example of a case where we can pick a proxy failure which basically requires the model to do all the same steps that it would have done for the real failure, and then do something visible at the end.

items.claim: Prefers explicitly not trying to hide that the model is in an eval over requiring indistinguishable proxy settings, because that constraint would make proxy construction far harder and the eval is meant to measure oversight adequacy, not model naivety.
items.quote: Note that we aren’t trying to prevent our models from knowing that they’re in an eval. A lot of these settings will involve things that are clearly for the sake of evaluating a model’s ability to stage a coup. It would be much harder to construct proxy settings if they also had to be indistinguishable from the settings where we expected to rely on the model’s outputs.

items.claim: Distrusts sandwiching evaluations because a misaligned model can exploit slack to behave well where developers have held-out information and badly elsewhere, so good results may overstate oversight quality.
items.quote: a misaligned model might be able to sabotage a sandwiching evaluations by purposefully giving good answers in domains where it knows that its developers have access to held out information, and answer much worse in cases where it knows we don't have access to the held out information.

items.claim: Prefers directly training the model toward the bad behavior (adversarial elicitation) over waiting to observe whether it does so naturally, because this removes slack the model could use to hide and gives measurable evidence.
items.quote: This problem doesn’t arise with the adversarial oversight evaluations, because we directly train the model to adopt policies which are bad according to our held-out information, which removes the slack that the model could have used to behave well even though it wasn’t being forced to by oversight.

items.claim: Constructs analogous test settings by finding a similar setting with strictly more ground-truth information and restricting the overseer to the information available in the real setting (sandwich, backtesting).
items.quote: you can construct an analogous setting by picking a similar situation where you have access to much more information, and then restricting the overseer to the information which you have access to in the setting of interest.

items.claim: Treats failure of a strong red team to produce undetected bad policies as evidence of adequacy only when proxy validity and capability elicitation hold, so negative results are conditional on those assumptions.
items.quote: I claim that if those conditions hold, then if you can’t train your models to demonstrate the proxy failures without looking bad to oversight, you’ve demonstrated local adequacy of oversight.

items.claim: Notes that non-constructive evaluations such as inconsistency tests only give one-sided evidence and must be combined with ground-truth evaluations.
items.quote: Note that even if you demonstrate that it’s impossible to train egregiously inconsistent models in a setting, you haven’t demonstrated that oversight is locally adequate—perhaps the oversight forces models to answer questions incorrectly in one particular way.

items.claim: Believes that at crunch time alignment work will be based on direct measurement via evals rather than long-range extrapolation, and wants researchers to practice eval-based technique iteration now.
items.quote: It seems likely to me that at crunch time, the core workflow of alignment practitioners will involve iterating on alignment techniques based on direct measurement of their effect on the evaluations that are used in safety arguments

items.claim: Runs evaluations separately per deployment use-case because failure modes and oversight difficulties differ between settings.
items.quote: We think it will probably make sense to run these evaluations separately for different AI use-cases, so that you can adjust the oversight process separately based on the problems identified by these evaluations.

items.claim: Open problem: formalizing the evaluation for recursive oversight setups; fallback is a common-sense 'I know it when I see it' adjudication of red-team success.
items.quote: None of these problems seem impossible to overcome, and it also seems plausible that we can just adopt a “I know it when I see it” approach to deciding whether the red team has exhibited a real problem.
